📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning.
  • Maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with plans, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

Maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

Sources indicate that in fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

Sources indicate that if you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

With that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

According to recent reports, so what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A major factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

According to recent reports, if you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

According to recent reports, if you’re up for ideas, start here. If you’re feeling low, jump to How to deal with spending Christmas alone when hard feelings come up.

If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

According to recent reports, 💙 Want some guidance for those few minutes? Settle into the Mornings meditation on Calm.

It has been revealed that 2. Cook or order the meal you really want: Skip the turkey-and-trimmings unless you love them. Go for whatever you're craving, whether that’s a roast for one, pancakes at noon, or your go-to takeout. Choosing food you’re excited about can turn an ordinary meal into a treat.

💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

Industry observers note that 5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

💙 Discover ten self-love activities to improve your well-being.

If you’d like to spend the day out of the house, these ideas include solo outings and activities around other people. Holiday hours often change and volunteer spots fill up, so check details as early as you can..

6. Spend time somewhere green: Stroll along a park path or trail, or find a bench and settle in for a while. Time in green space has been shown to quiet a busy mind. In one study, adults who walked for 90 minutes in nature reported less rumination (the looping, negative thinking that can feed low moods) than those who walked along a busy road.

💙 Ready to step outside? Try Calm’s Nature Walk meditation with Dr. Eric López to soak in the sights, sounds, and smells around you.

7. Volunteer for a few hours: Soup kitchens, shelters, and animal rescues often need extra hands on Christmas Day. Volunteering connects you with people who share a purpose, and research suggests performing acts of kindness may boost your well-being.

Industry observers note that 💙 Feeling the urge to give back? Tune into the Random Acts of Kindness meditation on Calm to see how small gestures add up.

In a recent development, 8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

Sources indicate that 9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

In a recent development, 10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a new trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

Recent findings suggest that there are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

Send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:.

Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

It has been revealed that you can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

It has been revealed that 💙 Not sure where to start? Explore Redefining Traditions with therapist Kati Morton on Calm.

Industry observers note that if you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

💙 Press play on the Loving-Kindness meditation on Calm.

Industry observers note that give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

Recent findings suggest that even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

Other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

If the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”.

💙 Practice being a Friend on the Inside with Jeff Warren on Calm.

It has been revealed that if you’re missing someone this Christmas, the day can feel especially tender. You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

It’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

According to recent reports, if your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

If you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

Recent findings suggest that it’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Proposal the day around what appeals to you.

In a recent development, if you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

If you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a new spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

If you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

In a recent development, it’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday plans is one way to look after yourself.

Sources indicate that A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a newly introduced ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

Latest Update: Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, mentioned:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

#160715. Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Industry observers note that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Industry observers note that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack. The chest tightness has eased, the shaking has stopped, and your breathing feels more steady. But instead of relief, there’s a strange exhaustion settling in, like you just ran a marathon you don’t remember signing up for. This is often called a panic attack hangover.

Recent findings suggest that the hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting. You might experience headaches, sore muscles, difficulty concentrating, or an overwhelming need to crash. These symptoms can feel alarming if no one ever mentioned they might show up, but they’re actually a normal part of the body’s recovery process.

Understanding what’s happening can ease some of the worry, and having a few gentle tools on hand can make the aftermath feel a little less isolating. Here’s what to know about panic attack hangovers, along with research-backed tips to support yourself through them.

A panic attack hangover is the period of lingering after-effects that follow a panic attack. Even though the rush of fear and physical symptoms has eased, your body can still feel off-balance for hours or even days afterward. Many people describe it as feeling strangely similar to an alcohol hangover: foggy, heavy, and emotionally sensitive.

According to recent reports, the experience can be unsettling, especially if you didn’t expect panic to have an “aftermath.” But panic attack hangovers are both common and temporary. They’re simply your body’s way of recovering from an intense stress response.

In a recent development, note: This guide focuses on panic attacks. If you’ve had an anxiety attack, which builds more gradually, read How to manage symptoms and find ease after an anxiety attack instead.

In a recent development, while panic attack hangovers can happen at any time, the effects aren’t the same for everyone. Still, there are some common symptoms people notice after a panic attack, some more frequently than others.

Fatigue or exhaustion: You might feel like your body’s battery has been completely drained.

Brain fog: You could find it hard to focus, remember things, or think clearly.

Muscle tension or soreness: Your jaw, shoulders, or chest might feel tight, achy, or tender from holding too much stress.

Emotional sensitivity: You may notice yourself crying more easily or feeling unusually fragile in everyday situations.

Headaches: You might experience pressure or pain often triggered by stress, shallow breathing, or unconscious clenching.

Digestive issues: You could have nausea, stomach discomfort, or sudden changes in your appetite that don’t seem to track.

Sleepiness or difficulty sleeping: You may find yourself crashing hard into deep rest or lying awake because you’re unable to settle down.

These symptoms usually fade within a day, although they can last longer depending on the amount of sleep you get, your stress levels, and your overall health. If they’re frequent or overwhelming, though, it may be a sign to get additional support.

It has been revealed that the reason panic leaves a hangover comes down to how your body handles stress. A panic attack sends your nervous system into full alert: your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles tighten. This is an ancient survival mechanism that’s been designed to keep you safe in an emergency.

The problem? Even when the threat isn’t real, your body still goes through the motions without an outlet to use up that surge of energy.

In a recent development, once the attack ends, your system shifts into recovery mode. That crash can leave you feeling shaky, sore, and depleted… much like finishing an intense workout. On top of that, the emotional weight of the experience—fear, vulnerability, or the worry it might happen again—can keep your brain buzzing even while your body’s trying to rest.

This combination of physical exhaustion and emotional strain creates the foggy, heavy state that many people call a panic attack hangover.

Panic attack hangovers can hit you hard, and you may not have the energy to do much after. These ideas are simple, low-lift, and designed for the days when everything feels like just too much.

Pick what’s doable today and ignore the rest: your nervous system will get the memo.

In a recent development, your body just ran an internal marathon, and it’s notable to be kind to it. If you can, postpone non-urgent tasks and try to give yourself a small recovery window.

Industry observers note that set a 10–15 minute timer, lie down or sit with support behind your back, and let your eyes rest. If you’re at work, try a short break, plus two minutes of slow breathing in a quiet corner. A pause can often help you recover faster.

Sources indicate that staying hydrated and keeping your blood sugar steady can help you feel more balanced as your body recovers from a panic attack. Dehydration and dips in blood sugar can make fatigue, headaches, and brain fog worse.

Drink water or an electrolyte beverage and have a simple snack, like fruit with nut butter, yogurt, or toast. This helps give your system some fuel to reset.

Recent findings suggest that slow, gentle breathing tells your nervous system that you’re safe. Try this for 2–3 minutes: Inhale through your nose for four counts, and then exhale through pursed lips for six or eight.

According to recent reports, longer exhales can help your nervous system shift from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest mode. But only do this if you feel comfortable. Don’t try to force anything.

Recent findings suggest that panic can cause you to tighten your muscles, especially in the jaw, chest, shoulders, and hands. Short, light movements help clear it all without overexertion.

You don’t have to do anything too intense. Simple shoulder rolls, gentle neck circles, a slow doorframe chest stretch, or a five-minute walk around the block or office floor can all help. If you’re seated, simply unclench your jaw, open and close your hands 10 times, or shake out your arms. The point is to loosen everything up.

Quick temperature shifts, like splashing cool water on your face or holding something cold, can help ground you and interrupt the leftover jitters after a panic attack.

This is because it’s actually a form of grounding that allows your nervous system to anchor itself back to the present moment.

Decision fatigue amplifies the brain fog that comes after a panic attack, so try to cut down on the number of choices you’re making.

Trim your to-do list to one or two essentials, and choose “good enough” over perfect. Reheat leftovers instead of cooking, tell your coworkers you’re running a little behind, and move all noncritical tasks to the next day. It sounds simple, but having that space will help more than you know.

Reduce stimulation to ease the post-panic attack stress. Dim overhead lights, switch to warm lamps, lower the volume on any music or background noise, and silence non-urgent notifications on your phone and laptop for an hour.

Sources indicate that if noise is unavoidable, try earplugs or a brown-noise playlist. If you enjoy aromatherapy a familiar scent (like lavender, vanilla, or eucalyptus) can also be grounding.

According to recent reports, writing a few lines about your feelings and symptoms post-panic attack can help your brain process what happened and move forward. Research highlights that journaling supports emotional regulation, which is why so many people find it useful for panic recovery, too — even if it’s just a quick note or voice memo.

Recent findings suggest that consider reflecting on what triggered your attack, what symptoms you noticed, what helped calm you down, and what you could do differently next time. This can help give you more effective coping tools for future attacks.

According to recent reports, reaching out, even with a simple text, helps calm the nervous system. Social support is one of the strongest buffers for stress recovery.

Industry observers note that send a text to someone you trust, simply asking to check in. If talking feels like too much, having someone just sit with you can also be helpful.

According to recent reports, after a panic attack, your system is more sensitive. Consider skipping or reducing how much caffeine you drink, as it can re-spark jitters. And avoid alcohol, as it’s been known to disrupt sleep and mood. Swap in decaf, herbal tea, or a half-caf and make sure to focus on nutrition and hydration to help support recovery.

Fatigue after a panic attack is real, and quality sleep helps reset your stress response. Keep bedtime predictable with a wind-down routine you enjoy, darken the room, and cool it slightly.

According to recent reports, if you desperately need a nap, cap it at 20–30 minutes, and avoid late-evening naps in order to protect nighttime sleep. If your mind spins when it’s time to go to bed, try a quiet meditation or body scan. This can help quiet the mind long enough to help you drift off faster.

Splash cold water on your face or run cool water over your wrists.

While you may not be able to prevent every spiral, it always helps to have something in your back pocket (literally) that helps you feel less alone and more ready.

Yes, a hangover can sometimes trigger panic attacks. This is because alcohol disrupts sleep, dehydrates your body, and causes blood sugar swings — and all of these effects can make your nervous system more sensitive the next day.

Alcohol also interferes with the neurotransmitters that regulate your mood, which can amplify feelings of unease or dread. If you’re already prone to anxiety, that extra stress can tip into panic.

Every person who drinks won’t necessarily have a panic attack, but if you notice a pattern between hangovers and panic, it may help to cut back, hydrate more intentionally, or avoid drinking on nights before demanding days.

Recent findings suggest that for most people, the hungover feeling eases within a few hours, but it’s not unusual for fatigue or brain fog to stretch into the next day. The duration of a panic attack hangover depends on several factors: how intense the panic attack was, how long it lasted, how well you slept, and what kind of support you gave your body afterward.

Industry observers note that try to find the recovery initiative that works best for you: getting enough water, food, gentle movement, and rest can speed up the reset. However, if you find that your hangover lasts longer than 24 hours or happens every time you panic, it may be a sign that your nervous system is under strain. In this case, getting some professional support can help.

In a recent development, brain fog and fatigue are your nervous system’s way of asking for recovery time, so supporting your body can make the fog lift faster. Start with water or an electrolyte drink, followed by a small, balanced meal or snack. Light movement like walking or stretching also helps by boosting circulation and clearing leftover stress hormones, while short breaks from screens give your brain a reset.

It has been revealed that some people find that changing environments—stepping outside for fresh air, moving to a quieter space, or dimming harsh lighting—makes a noticeable difference in clarity. Rest is important, too, but you don’t want to overdo it. A short nap capped at 20–30 minutes usually helps more than staying in bed for hours.

The exhaustion you feel after a panic attack is the crash that comes after an adrenaline surge. Basically, when you panic, your body burns through enormous amounts of energy in a short time. Your heart rate rises, your muscles tense, and your brain goes into overdrive to scan for danger.

According to recent reports, even though there isn’t an actual threat, your body doesn’t know that, so it uses up its resources as if there is. Once the panic attack passes, your hormones shift, and your body needs to come down from the emotional intensity. While it’s easy to look at this exhaustion as weakness, it’s really just your body’s way of recovering from an all-systems-on alert. That’s why gentleness is key for recovery.

In a recent development, you can’t always prevent panic attacks, but you can definitely soften the after-effects. The most helpful strategies are proactive, or preventing one before it comes on. Think: getting consistent sleep, eating balanced meals to keep blood sugar steady, staying hydrated, and limiting alcohol or excessive caffeine.

Industry observers note that some people find it useful to have a short aftercare routine ready, too, such as hydrating, stretching, or texting a friend once the panic subsides. This helps to prevent the hangover from stretching out longer than necessary.

Over time, therapy and skills training can also reduce both the frequency of panic attacks and the severity of hangovers. You’ll essentially learn how to give your nervous system a softer landing.

Recent findings suggest that headaches and sore muscles are common after a panic attack. During panic, your jaw, neck, shoulders, and chest may tighten without you noticing, and fast, shallow breathing could add to the headache.

Recent findings suggest that unclenching your jaw, rolling your shoulders, or holding a cool compress to your forehead may help. Get care right away if you have a sudden, severe headache, chest pain, numbness or weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. If your headache lasts longer than you’d expect, check in with your doctor or primary care provider.

After a panic attack, give your body a few minutes to settle before you do anything else. Stay where you are if it’s safe, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.

Shakiness or fog is a normal part of coming down from panic, so you don’t need to push through it. Once the first wave passes, tell someone you trust what happened and lower the demands on yourself for the rest of the day. The 12 tips above have ideas for the hours that follow. If panic attacks keep happening, talking with a doctor or mental health professional may help.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a fresh attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone upcoming.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, showed a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also showed a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

How to write your retirement message or announcement at work

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that retirement is the end of an era.
  • Sources indicate that to bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time.
  • Nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that retirement is the end of an era. And while it’s thrilling to finally have time to do all the things you’ve been meaning to do, leaving behind your coworkers, especially if you’re close, can feel bittersweet.

Sources indicate that to bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time. But what do you say? How can you possibly sum up years of collaboration, chaos, and connection in just a few sentences?

Nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with. By adapting them to fit your specific role and personality, you can acknowledge the relationships that mattered, offer an authentic goodbye, and leave with intention. Happy retirement!

You might think that your retirement messages need to be a perfect balance of professional, funny, and sweet, but what’s most key is that you sound like yourself.

To ensure that your note is polished and professional, keep these tips in mind.

Most people don’t want to read a long email, no matter who it’s from. A few honest lines work perfectly.

Recent findings suggest that “The time has come. After 12 years of wearing the same pants four out of five days of the week and drinking lukewarm coffee from the break room, I’m retiring. I’ve truly loved working with you and appreciate every wild and wonderful day we shared.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Before I officially retire, I wanted to say thank you for this beautiful ride. You’ve all been unforgettable and lovely to me. You’re the reason this job didn’t feel like work.”.

According to recent reports, “After 18 years, I’ve officially graduated to more peaceful days filled with puzzles and midday naps. Logging off now, grateful for every moment. I will miss you all!”.

Sources indicate that 💙 As you head into retirement, reflect on all the good times you had at work. Gratitude for the Day with Chibs Okereke can help you tap into those positive feelings.

Gratitude makes goodbye messages feel a little warmer. Think about the people or experiences that left a mark, like the coworker who knew your coffee order by heart or the one who always lent you their umbrella when it was raining. (If you need some more guidance, here are eight tips to cultivate an attitude of gratitude.).

“I want to thank my chosen family who made this workplace so special. Your support, humor, and occasional emergency snack stashes got me through some tough days and made the good ones even better.”.

It has been revealed that “Thanks to everyone who made me feel welcome, challenged, and appreciated. You’re the reason I stayed as long as I did. Well, that, and Barbara’s famous cheesecake. I’ll miss you all (almost as much as I’ll miss all the cake).”.

“A heartfelt thank you to my team — you made me better every day. I’m so lucky I got to be a player on this incredible squad. Rooting for all of you always. Can’t wait to hear about all that you accomplish.”.

In a recent development, A little story can go a long way. In addition to reminding people of the good times, it can make your message feel more original. You don’t have to write a novel, and it doesn’t need to be profound — just aim for real.

“I’ll never forget the power outage of 2019 when we all played trashcan basketball while waiting for the lights to come back on. We made the best out of a tough situation, and that speaks to the type of amazing people you are. Please stay in touch!”.

Sources indicate that “Monday mornings just won’t be the same without our doughnut runs. Thanks for the memories, team.”.

Industry observers note that let people know all that you’ve learned while working and what you’ll carry forward. Not only will this help fill up your cup, but it can also remind people what they’ve learned while working with you. (Here are 20 questions to help with any potential writer’s block.).

“This job taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and that I don’t need to talk louder while I’m on zoom. (Still working on that one…) But most of all, it reminded me how amazing it is to work with such loyal, thoughtful people. I’ll never forget it. Thank you.”.

“Beyond the spreadsheets and deadlines, I’m leaving with lifelong friendships, a few more well-earned wrinkles, and countless memories.”.

“This place taught me how to lead, how to listen, and how to troubleshoot a broken coffee machine under pressure.”.

Some words of encouragement, a simple goodbye, or even a little glimpse of what’s next for you can be a sweet way to sign off.

“I’m off to spend more time traveling, playing with my grandkids, and mastering the art of sourdough once and for all. Wishing you all continued success — and a little less time in meetings.”.

In a recent development, “Wishing you all smooth launches, strong coffee, and at least one good laugh a day. Keep crushing it.”.

“I’ll be around — probably in sweatpants, gardening gloves, or both. Don’t be a stranger.”.

💙 Consider listening to Endings with Tamara Levitt if you’re having a hard time saying goodbye to your work and the people you’ve met there.

It has been revealed that it can be tempting to sneak out, but saying farewell to your coworkers is a kind thing to do — and it can help you too. Here’s why:.

In a recent development, 1. It gives you closure on your terms: Retirement can be a tough transition. One day, you have 50 emails and several meetings, and the next, your inbox is at zero, and you have nothing but time on your hands. Writing a goodbye message can help you mark the transition.

In a recent development, 2. It opens the door for real connection: When you write a farewell message, you’re inviting people to respond. What better way to leave than by clearly seeing the impact you had on your coworkers?

3. It lets you shape your own legacy: Your goodbye message can be a tiny chance to shape how people remember you. Go out on a positive note — literally.

Industry observers note that 💙 Writing to a coworker who’s retiring? These retirement wishes can help you find the right words.

Industry observers note that an announcement and a goodbye note do different jobs. The announcement shares your news and your last day. The thank-yous and memories from the tips above can follow it.

Manager first: Tell your manager before anyone else, so the news doesn’t reach them through a group email.

Timing: If you can, send the announcement a few weeks before your last day so people have time to say goodbye.

Subject line: Use a clear one, like “My retirement news.”.

Opening lines: Lead with the news, then name who will cover your work.

Long tenure: If you’ve been at the organization for decades, add a sentence or two about your time there, and keep the news first.

Here’s an example for someone who’s been at a company for a long time: “I started here 30 years ago, and my last day will be March 31. Over the next few weeks, I’ll be handing off my projects to Marcus and wrapping up my open work. If you’d like to catch up before I go, please grab time on my calendar. I’d love to see as many of you as I can.”.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to send a retirement message, but it can be one of the simplest ways to wrap up this chapter with a bit of closure and grace. After all, you’ve spent a lot of time with these people over the years.

Writing a short, thoughtful message can help you leave on a kind note. You might also be surprised at how meaningful even a few lines can feel, both for you and the people reading them.

According to recent reports, there’s no one right way to send a retirement message. If you want to keep it casual, you could say something like, “After 15 years, I’m off to find out if daytime TV lives up to the hype. Thanks for the talks, laughs, and memories.”.

A more heartfelt message you could send is: “It’s been a true honor to work alongside so many talented people. I’m leaving with deep gratitude for my time here — and for all of you.”.

Industry observers note that if humor’s more your vibe, you could say: “Today’s my last day. Thanks for the memories — and for being so nice about the fact that I was always muted on Zoom. You’d think after a few years, I’d learn my lesson, but I digress. You’re the best, and I’ll miss you.”.

In a recent development, your tone depends on your personality and your workplace culture. If you’re in a very professional environment, a more formal message is the best way to go, but if your usual emails include memes and inside jokes, it’s okay to joke around.

Sources indicate that in general, the best retirement messages usually sound like the person writing them, so trust your voice and just be yourself. You’ve earned the right to say goodbye on your terms.

There isn’t a standard checklist, but here are a few good touchpoints that can help you find your flow:.

Mention a funny or heartfelt memory.

Share a bit about what you’ve learned on the job.

Consider sprinkling in your future aims.

Close with a simple and warm goodbye.

According to recent reports, yes. Email is often preferred in the workplace, as it allows you to reach everyone and provides people with an opportunity to reply.

Whether you send it to your whole team or just a few close coworkers, an email is a low-stress, high-impact way to say farewell. Just remember to hit “send” before IT cuts your access!

It has been revealed that if you’re retiring, your thank-you message to colleagues works best when it says who you’re thanking and what they did for you. You can add it to your retirement announcement or send it as a separate note.

Industry observers note that for the whole team, a few lines are enough: “Thank you all for the patience and the laughs. Working with this team has been the best part of my job.” For one person, name something specific: “Dana, thank you for answering my questions in my first year. I couldn’t have learned this job without you.” If coworkers gave you a send-off or a gift, a short note afterward can say thanks again.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.
  • Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.
  • First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.

First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

Recent findings suggest that this sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

Recent findings suggest that finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

Industry observers note that it’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to plan. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:.

Recent findings suggest that what these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most vital distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

According to recent reports, vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution initiative balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

In a recent development, fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

According to recent reports, the IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

Recent findings suggest that the average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sources indicate that if you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

According to recent reports, yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

According to recent reports, generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

In a recent development, it is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.

Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches. How do I know if the stomachaches are related to anxiety or a medical condition? How do I know when to see a doctor?”.

Industry observers note that as parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance. Here are a few ways to tell the difference, and clear signs that it’s time to seek medical help.

According to recent reports, understand the mind-body connection. Our gut and brain are in constant conversation. When a child feels overwhelmed, scared, or worried, their body will respond with stomach pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and a generalized discomfort. These symptoms are not imagined or exaggerated; they are physical reactions to emotional stress.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

Observe timing and patterns. When are stomachaches happening? Stomach pain related to anxiety trends to show up during specific times: before and around school, tests, social events, and bedtime. Does your child’s stomachache dissipate after these types of events, or when they are comforted or distracted?

It has been revealed that are your child’s stomach pains taking place at night? Are they making it difficult for your child to eat? Are they losing weight? Is your child experiencing chronic diarrhea or do they have blood in their stool? Are they vomiting? These symptoms are more indicative of an underlying medical condition, especially if they become worse over time.

Keep a log. Track when your child has stomach pains to help you discern whether it’s due to anxiety or an underlying medical condition. Occasional stomachaches that happen during stressful times are common.

However, if your child complains of a stomachache several times each week for more than a month, consult with your pediatrician or seek a gastroenterologist.

[Read: “5 Ways to Reframe Anxiety for Your Worried Teen”].

And remember: You don’t have to choose between taking anxiety seriously and taking physical symptoms seriously. Both deserve attention. By watching for patterns, listening carefully, and seeking help when needed, you’re doing exactly what your child needs: letting them know that any pain they experience matters.

Liz Nissim, Ph.D., is a clinical and school psychologist specializing in parenting and executive function coaching for neurodivergent children and teens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two upcoming studies suggest autism and ADHD are becoming better recognized, not actually more prevalent, and that executive function and social challenges seen in both conditions actually stem from different underlying brain mechanisms.

ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) share overlapping symptoms, and prior studies suggest that nearly half of autistic children also have ADHD.1 Now, two fresh studies on ADHD and ASD profiles suggest that rising diagnosis rates are a product of improved symptom recognition and diagnostic practices, and that executive function and social impairments seen in both ADHD and ASD may be traced to different cognitive pathways.

Industry observers note that the first study, published in JAMA Psychiatry,2 evaluated the health records of 71,000 children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and 713,000 controls; it found that the annual number of individuals in the nationwide Danish health registry with newly diagnosed ADHD and/or ASD increased from 4,944 in 2012 to 9,179 in 2022. The proportion of girls diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and the median age at diagnosis also grew during the 10-year study period from 2012 to 2022.

Sources indicate that however, traditional risk factors strongly linked to an ADHD or ASD diagnosis in 2012, such as low birth weight or lower household income, have become progressively less predictive with time. For example, children born with a low birth weight were 54% more likely to receive a subsequent diagnosis of ADHD or ASD in 2012; by 2022, that percentage dropped to 17%. Overall, the study found that children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD today more closely resemble their neurotypical peers compared to those diagnosed 10 years ago.

Sources indicate that these findings do not mean that ADHD or ASD has become less impairing; the spectrum of cases has shifted as clinicians get better at identifying less obvious cases. Greater awareness of ADHD and ASD, and broader access to diagnostic assessment tools, are also factors contributing to growing diagnoses among children.

It has been revealed that “The study results do not show that these conditions are being overdiagnosed, or that they have become less severe,” indicates Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, Ph.D., a senior author of the study. “Rather, they indicate that the population receiving these diagnoses has changed over time, and this needs to be taken into account when interpreting current trends.”.

The second, smaller study, published in Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry,3 found that executive functioning (EF) and social cognition (SC) impairments in children diagnosed with ADHD or ASD may look similar, but the impairments stem from different underlying mechanisms.

The cross-sectional, four-year study analyzed performance-based measures of 123 children, aged 6 to 11 years, across three matched groups: mild ASD, combined-type ADHD, and neurotypical peers.

Findings indicated that both ADHD and ASD groups performed worse than their neurotypical peers on measures of EF and SC. However, children with ADHD demonstrated weak social cognition due to difficulties with response inhibition and attention. Social cognition weaknesses in children with ASD, on the other hand, appeared to result from difficulties in understanding and interpreting social information.

More specifically, children in the ASD group performed significantly worse than children with ADHD on measures of:.

Children with ASD also displayed more difficulties than did children with ADHD on executive function tasks that measured the ability to shift between rules and adapt strategies.

Children in the ADHD group performed significantly worse than those in the ASD group on measures of:.

How executive functions related to social cognition across disorders was the strongest indication of different cognitive processes between the two clinical groups. In the ADHD group, the theory-of-mind model explained 72% of the variance, compared to just 55% in the ASD group.

According to recent reports, the researchers surmise that a person with ADHD relies heavily on executive functions, such as inhibition, auditory attention, and design fluency, for social cognition. In essence, their difficulties in social situations are not because they don’t understand social concepts but because distractions and impulsivity interfere.

In the ASD group, social difficulties were more likely to stem from affect recognition (understanding facial cues) and response set (cognitive flexibility, shifting perspectives), rather than from attention deficit or impulse control.

Sources indicate that “ADHD and autism are two separate and distinct conditions that happen to be found together much more frequently than would be expected by chance alone,” claims ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. “For people with co-existing ADHD and ASD, treating the ADHD is a means to an end. The world is a classroom for people with ASD, and they have to be ready to observe and practice what they’ve learned.”.

Results from the study suggest individuals would benefit more from targeted ADHD and ASD interventions matched to each disorder-specific profile rather than a single shared approach.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that you probably don’t give much thought to how your heart speeds up during exercise or how blood continues flowing to your brain when you stand up.
  • The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, blood pressure, the digestive process, body temperature, and continuous blood circulation in the presence of gravity — squeezing blood out of the legs and torso and redistributing it to the head and heart when you move from lying down or sitting to standing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The autonomic nervous system regulates everything from heart rate to digestion. Abnormalities may contribute to ADHD and POTS symptoms.

It has been revealed that you probably don’t give much thought to how your heart speeds up during exercise or how blood continues flowing to your brain when you stand up. These essential functions are managed by the autonomic nervous system, the body’s complex operating system, which runs quietly in the background.

The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, blood pressure, the digestive process, body temperature, and continuous blood circulation in the presence of gravity — squeezing blood out of the legs and torso and redistributing it to the head and heart when you move from lying down or sitting to standing.

Some studies suggest that autonomic nervous system abnormalities may contribute to ADHD symptoms like inattention and impulsiveness. Clinicians may notice and use these symptoms to diagnose ADHD, but the underlying cause might reflect atypical autonomic nervous system activity.

Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is an atypical or malfunctioning state of the autonomic nervous system. People with ADHD and/or hypermobility appear to have a higher prevalence of POTS than do members of the general population. Symptoms include dizziness or fainting when standing up from a sitting or lying position due to sudden changes in blood pressure and heart rate.

[Read: ADHD’s Curious Connections to Chronic Inflammation and Dysautonomia].

In individuals with hypermobility, autonomic dysregulation may be caused by irritation of the nerves that are intermittently stretched due to lax ligaments at the craniocervical junction, where the brain and upper spine meet.

A tilt table test, which measures your heart rate and blood pressure as you change position, is the main way POTS is diagnosed. Other assessments include blood and urine tests and a measure of the autonomic nerves that control sweating.

[Read: Exploring the ADHD-Inflammation Link].

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Small acts of kindness and self-compassion can interrupt a cycle of self-criticism and release neurotransmitters that create a sense of wellbeing.

In a recent development, some years ago, my daughter was beaten up at a kids’ gathering. I asked myself as a psychologist, “What happened to kindness? When did we lose it?”.

In a recent development, I started to dig into the research. In the World Happiness Report, researchers looked at kindness as a factor contributing to happiness, and they developed a novel way to study the prevalence of kind acts. They tracked “lost” wallets to see if they were returned. They found that more people were helping strangers than was reported before the pandemic, which may be surprising.

Recent findings suggest that other social science studies found that measurably happier people live in areas where community members tend to donate more, volunteer their time, or help strangers. In other words, helping inspires more helping.

[Download: Get a Grip on Tough Emotions].

What explains this kindness-happiness connection? In short, giving or receiving kindness kickstarts a “helper’s high” in our brains.

Research highlights that acts of kindness engage certain brain networks that release good chemicals like an internal pharmacy:.

According to recent reports, the dopamine from a helper’s high is different from the endorphin hit associated with running, gaming, or gambling, which keeps you wanting more. The dopamine generated in a helper’s high continues to produce positive feelings over time. The release of these neurotransmitters is especially helpful for people with ADHD who may struggle with emotional control, motivation, and stress.

Recent findings suggest that studies have shown that volunteering, even for one hour a week, can reduce inflammatory and stress cortisol responses, and even increase longevity. Volunteering is also considered a preventative action for loneliness and depression. Teens who volunteer outside their homes are more resilient and less likely to become depressed, according to research.

Helping people learn to be kind to themselves is my lifelong challenge as a clinical psychologist. We tend to prioritize other people’s needs over our own. But the research is clear on self-compassion: When you talk to yourself in a kinder way, or do kind things for yourself, you’re learning how to quiet that inner critic.

[Read: Self-Compassion: The New ADHD Treatment].

5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)
