💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing.
  • It has been revealed that essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing. You reach for the small bottle of lavender essential oil on your desk, hold it a few inches from your nose, and breathe in slowly. Your shoulders drop, and the list feels a little more manageable.

It has been revealed that essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings. When worries pile up, a quick ritual like that can sound appealing. Still, it’s worth asking how much these oils can really do for anxiety.

Ahead, we’ll cover what the research indicates about essential oils for anxiety, and how to try them at home.

Recent findings suggest that essential oils are concentrated plant extracts. Makers draw the aromatic compounds out of flowers, leaves, bark, peel, or resin, usually by steaming or pressing the plant. What’s left is a potent oil that carries the plant’s scent.

According to recent reports, aromatherapy is the practice of using these scents to ease stress and lift your mood. When you inhale a scent, the molecules reach receptors high in your nose that connect to the limbic system, a part of the brain involved in emotion and memory. That link is one reason a smell can bring back a memory or shift your mood before you've had time to think.

Essential oils may take the edge off anxiety, but think of them as a comfort alongside established treatments, not a substitute for them.

A 2023 systematic review pooled dozens of randomized trials and found that essential oils lowered both in-the-moment and overall anxiety levels compared with unscented oil or usual care.

Early results look promising, though they come with a few caveats. Most of those trials were small, and many measured anxiety in medical settings, such as the nervous stretch before surgery, rather than the everyday worry most people deal with. Results also varied widely from study to study.

If your anxiety is intense and disruptive to your daily life, talk with a doctor or therapist.

Sources indicate that 💙 Not sure if it’s stress or anxiety? Here’s how to tell the difference.

Sources indicate that some essential oils have far more anxiety research behind them than others. These five come up most often in studies and in aromatherapy practice. Your scent preference matters here, so you might respond to one oil and not another. Start with the one that appeals to you most.

Lavender smells floral and herbal, with a clean, slightly woody edge. It’s the most studied oil for anxiety by a wide margin, and its main compound, linalool, may help calm the nervous system.

In a recent development, A lavender oil capsule called Silexan was tested in a 10-week trial of adults with generalized anxiety disorder, where it reduced anxiety more than a placebo capsule. Since Silexan is swallowed rather than inhaled, the results say little about lavender aromatherapy.

If you’re new to essential oils, lavender is a gentle place to start: its scent is familiar to most people, and it’s widely available.

In a recent development, neroli comes from the blossom of the bitter orange tree, Citrus aurantium. Its scent is sweet and floral, with only a hint of citrus.

According to recent reports, in the 2023 meta-analysis, bitter orange oil ranked at or near the top of the oils tested for both in-the-moment and overall anxiety. It didn’t clearly outperform lavender, though, and far fewer trials back it up.

Unlike bergamot and other citrus peel oils, neroli hasn’t shown sun-sensitivity problems. Even so, as with any oil, dilute it and patch-test first (see the safety notes below).

It has been revealed that rose, often sold as Damask rose oil, smells sweet and floral. In the same 2023 review, it was the second most studied oil after lavender. Rose oil was linked to lower in-the-moment anxiety, mostly in trials of people facing medical procedures.

Pure rose oil is one of the pricier options, since it takes a mountain of petals to make a small bottle. Fortunately, a little goes a long way, and a few drops in a diffuser can scent a room.

Chamomile oil smells soft, warm, and a little like apple, which suits an evening wind-down.

In a randomized trial, older adults who inhaled chamomile oil for a month had lower anxiety scores than those who received a placebo.

In a separate hospital trial, people with heart conditions who breathed in chamomile oil for two nights had lower anxiety than those given an unscented oil.

Bergamot is the citrus that gives Earl Grey tea its signature scent: fresh and zesty, with a softer, sweeter edge.

It has been revealed that in one randomized controlled trial, people in treatment for substance use were given bergamot aromatherapy. They reported lower anxiety than those who received standard care alone.

Recent findings suggest that bergamot and other citrus peel oils can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you apply them to your skin, keep that area out of direct sun for a day or so.

There are several ways to use essential oils, so try a few and see what works for you. Here are the four main methods:.

Diffuse: Add a few drops of oil and water to an electric diffuser to scent a room. This gentle method suits a bedroom or home office.

Inhale: Hold the bottle a few inches from your nose and take a slow breath. You can also put a drop on a tissue and smell that instead.

In a recent development, apply to skin: Always dilute essential oil before it touches your skin. Mix a few drops into a carrier oil, such as jojoba or coconut, then rub a little on your wrists, temples, or the back of your neck. If you’d rather skip the mixing, pre-diluted rollers are a convenient option.

In a recent development, add to a bath or shower: For a bath, mix a few drops into a carrier oil or unscented bath base, then pour it into warm water. For a shower, put a few drops on the shower floor, away from the running water, and let the steam carry the scent. Oil can make the floors slippery, so step in carefully.

💙 At bedtime, turn on your diffuser and listen to The Lavender Valley, a Sleep Story on Calm that follows a stroll toward a heavenly scent.

Industry observers note that buy from a reputable brand, since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t check essential oils for purity or strength.

Patch-test first: dab diluted oil on a small area of skin and wait 24 hours to check for redness or itching.

Avoid direct sun on skin where you’ve applied citrus peel oils, like bergamot, because they can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

Don’t swallow essential oils without guidance from a qualified healthcare professional.

Keep essential oils away from children and pets, since some oils are toxic to animals.

Check with your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or managing a health condition, as some oils aren't recommended.

Aromatherapy can be one part of a wider wellness routine. Use oils alongside other habits that may help with anxiety, like gentle movement, breathing exercises, time outside, and meditation. For instance, smelling lavender before a guided meditation can help you settle in.

💙 To round out your routine, explore these six natural ways to ease anxiety.

💙 Pair your aromatherapy with Calming Anxiety, a five-minute breathing meditation on Calm.

Lavender is the most studied oil for anxiety, which makes it a popular first pick. That said, scent preference matters, so the oil you enjoy most may suit you best. Neroli, rose, chamomile, and bergamot are also common choices, with some research to support them.

Industry observers note that essential oils may help you feel less anxious, and studies have found a modest calming effect, especially in stressful moments. However, the research is limited, especially for everyday anxiety.

If your anxiety feels frequent or intense, or if you’re having panic attacks, reach out to a doctor or therapist for support. Oils can be one small part of your routine, but they can’t replace medication or therapy.

You can put diluted essential oil on pulse points, like your wrists, temples, the back of your neck, or behind your ears, where body warmth helps release the scent. Mix the oil into a carrier oil first, and avoid putting citrus oils on skin that will be in direct sun.

At home, you can diffuse a few drops of essential oil, inhale from the bottle, apply diluted oil to your skin, or add an oil blend to a bath. Pick the method that fits your space and routine.

Frankincense is a popular choice for relaxation, but research on its effects on people is still limited. Most of the evidence comes from animal studies on one of its compounds, incensole acetate, which reduced anxious behavior in mice. If you enjoy its warm, woody scent, it may still be worth trying.

Recent findings suggest that aromatherapy uses essential oils on purpose, while smelling something nice can mean anything pleasant, from fresh-baked bread to your favorite candle. With aromatherapy, you can pick a scent and diffuse it or breathe it in from the bottle. Both can lift your mood, but aromatherapy makes smelling the scent a habit.

It has been revealed that essential oils can irritate sensitive skin, so it helps to dilute them in a carrier oil and patch test first. If you have a skin condition like eczema, ask your doctor before trying aromatherapy, or skip skin contact and use a diffuser instead.

Recent findings suggest that international Essential Oils Day is on July 11 every year. It’s a day to celebrate essential oils and the ways people use them for well-being. If you’ve been curious about aromatherapy, it’s a good time to try it.

You don’t need much to take part. Choose an essential oil that appeals to you, such as lavender or rose, and add a few drops to a diffuser. Then take in the scent with a few slow breaths or a short meditation. If you already use oils, you could try a newly introduced scent or build a wind-down habit around a favorite.

Breaking: Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • Sources indicate that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

Sources indicate that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

Industry observers note that that means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings crucial for this group.

Despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

Recent findings suggest that however, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

Sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

Sources indicate that sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

Compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Recent findings suggest that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

Recent findings suggest that our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or newly introduced life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a fresh job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

The struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a newly introduced schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

From the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

Sources indicate that transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A new job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

According to recent reports, “I don’t travel much,” claims Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

[Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

Recent findings suggest that most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.

The link was modest overall but stronger among girls and among teenagers.

Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Massive Research Findings

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
  • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
  • In a recent development, an estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

In a recent development, an estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: Latest Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

In clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

“These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John said. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

Many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

Industry observers note that “This raises a really vital question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John said. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

The experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John remarked.

[Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

In doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John noted.

Sources indicate that john’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

In a recent development, it’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

Recent findings suggest that this 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

Sources indicate that and lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

Sources indicate that this dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

Breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

Breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

There are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

Sources indicate that you may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

According to recent reports, helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

In a recent development, when life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

As one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

How to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

This type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

According to recent reports, how to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and quickly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

How to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

This technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

Sources indicate that how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

Recent findings suggest that alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

How to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

According to recent reports, this technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory problems. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

Sources indicate that the lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood quickly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

How to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

How to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

Breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

Recent findings suggest that practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

Many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

When anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

If you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

According to recent reports, if you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Industry observers note that surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

In fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to rapidly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a fresh study.
  • Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.
  • The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a fresh study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

In a recent development, study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings demonstrated that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

According to recent reports, premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

The study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

Researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

It has been revealed that the relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents said that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

Sources indicate that “I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, remarked. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”.

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” said Connie, another reader.

“I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” noted ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

“PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”.

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

According to recent reports, “Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”.

Industry observers note that the researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors said they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.

According to recent reports, 2 Team, A. E. (2025). PMDD and ADHD: Understanding the connection and managing symptoms. ADDA – Attention Deficit Disorder Association. https://add.org/pmdd-and-adhd/.

It has been revealed that 3 Pooja Thakrar, Kalyani Bhukar, Rajat Oswal, Premenstrual dysphoric disorder: Prevalence, quality of life and disability due to illness among medical and paramedical students. Closing the Skills Gap for Autistic Employees

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the unemployment rate for workers with autism is staggering.
  • In Australia, the unemployment rate for neurodivergent adults hovers around 34%, nearly eight times the national average.
  • ASA was established in 2020 to increase workforce participation among young neurodivergent adults by training them in substantial data for the geospatial and digital engineering fields, then placing them in corporate and government sectors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the unemployment rate for workers with autism is staggering. One Australian organization is aiming to change that.

In Australia, the unemployment rate for neurodivergent adults hovers around 34%, nearly eight times the national average. Clearly, there is a stigma around hiring neurodivergent people and it stems from a fear of the unknown. One not-for-profit company, Australian Spatial Analytics (ASA), is working to fix that.

ASA was established in 2020 to increase workforce participation among young neurodivergent adults by training them in substantial data for the geospatial and digital engineering fields, then placing them in corporate and government sectors. At ASA, we leverage these employees’ cognitive strengths — attention to detail, pattern recognition, laser-sharp focus, and innovative problem-solving skills, all of which are invaluable in these fields.

Recent findings suggest that about 80% of ASA’s staff identify as neurodivergent, which includes ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and dyspraxia. ASA’s recruitment process goes beyond conventional practices; it assesses potential candidates based on transferable skills, hobbies, and interests, rather than relying on formal qualifications or previous experience. Many of the new data analysts we have successfully placed in jobs are in paid positions for the first time.

[Read: We’re Hiring – ADHD-Friendly Careers].

Industry observers note that yet the analysts’ value to their employers is without questions. Executives have praised the ASA-trained analysts who have joined their companies, citing their work ethic, dedication, and problem-solving skills.

Recent findings suggest that during the job-seeking process, ASA provides candidates with sample interview questions 48 hours in advance to help minimize anxiety. Once hired, employees receive comprehensive and paid on-the-job training that includes soft skills like communication and self-advocacy coaching.

[Read: Nail Your Job Interview – 3 Strategies for Neurodivergent Applicants].

It has been revealed that based on our experience, creating a supportive and productive environment requires only minor accommodations. Flexible start and finish times, predictable routines, the option for hybrid work to reduce commuting stress, adjustable lighting, noise-canceling headphones, and direct communication make a profound difference, not only for neurodivergent people, but for everyone in the workplace.

To help change paradigms, ASA offers a Neurodiversity in the Workplace Training Program for other organizations. It covers neurodiversity awareness, plus effective strategies for communication, managing anxiety in the work environment, leading neurodiverse teams, and promoting neurodivergent inclusion.

Ultimately, our goal is to put ourselves out of business.

Karly Ischenko is a Human Resources Business Partner at Australian Spatial Analytics.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
  • People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.
  • A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results indicated that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, remarked:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very important to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This mentioned, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially key, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 50% of people receiving treatment for eating disorders, especially bulimia and binge-eating, may have ADHD, though few are diagnosed, according to a new study.

Roughly half of adults in treatment for eating disorders display symptoms of ADHD, though few are diagnosed, according to a upcoming cross-sectional study published in Journal of Eating Disorders.1.

Recent findings suggest that the study, conducted at Esquirol Hospital in Limoges, France, included 120 participants, 95.8% of whom were female. Using the ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS v1.1), researchers screened participants for ADHD, then followed up to confirm the screening with the Diagnostic Interview for ADHD (DIVA 2.0). More than half (61) of the participants met criteria for ADHD, according to these measures, though only two had received a prior diagnosis. Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder were more strongly associated with ADHD than was anorexia nervosa.

According to recent reports, participants who showed symptoms of ADHD also had more psychiatric comorbidities and higher rates of impulsivity, body dissatisfaction, and smoking and alcohol use. Personality assessments revealed that participants with ADHD symptoms showed greater dependence on rewards, while those who did not exhibited higher rates of self-regulation.

“These findings support ADHD screening and integrated treatments targeting impulsivity and attentional dysregulation,” wrote the study’s authors.

Sources indicate that in “ADHD and Eating Disorders: Research, Diagnosis & Treatment Guidelines,” Roberto Olivardia, Ph.D., explores the myriad biological and genetic factors that may predispose individuals with ADHD to eating disorders. They include:.

Further research is needed to understand all possible mechanisms, as well as the benefit of ADHD treatment on eating disorder recovery.

In an ADDitude guest blog post titled, “Dopamine, Not Discipline: The ADHD–Eating Disorder Link I Was Missing,” Penelope Mazzetti offers these insights: “My ‘out-of-control eating’ wasn’t an matter of willpower; it was partly sensory-seeking behavior, a well-documented ADHD trait. As ADHD brains like mine are chronically low in dopamine, we are wired to seek stimulation, and food just happens to be fast, legal, and always available.”.

1Bonilla, A., Torelli, S., Virevialle, AL. et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults with eating disorders: prevalence, clinical correlates, and personality profiles. J Eat Disord (2026). https://doi.org/10.1186/s40337-026-01793-6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, stated:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Industry observers note that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. Breaking: Why Kids with ADHD Get Stuck in the Screen-Time Loop. And How to Break It.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games.
  • According to recent reports, screen addiction is not the problem.
  • According to recent reports, once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games. Learn why ADHD brains get hooked on these “other stimulants,” and how to protect them.

According to recent reports, screen addiction is not the problem. Your child is not hooked on their phone, but rather the endless loop of novelty, stimulation, and unpredictable rewards streaming through it. It’s the dopamine; not the device.

According to recent reports, once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one. Here’s the central point: Phones and video games weren’t as addictive before they got connected to the Internet. A standalone game that you can beat has an ending. A connected game like Fortnite, Roblox, or Minecraft never ends.

Industry observers note that for a kid with ADHD, whose brain runs on a dopamine deficit, the Internet is impossible to resist – by design. We hand the most addictive delivery system ever built to the most vulnerable brains, and then ask them to show self-control. That’s not a fair fight.

Sources indicate that adolescents and teens with ADHD find screens irresistible, and it’s no wonder why. The ADHD brain is dopamine-deficient, and screens deliver dopamine instantly, reliably, and without effort. Almost everything else in life – school, sports, chores, homework – delivers dopamine slowly, inconsistently, and with lots of effort. The brain always chooses the path of least resistance to its dopamine.

This isn’t a character flaw or a discipline problem. It’s neurology. The dopamine hit from a connected screen is more powerful and more reinforcing for an ADHD brain than it is for a neurotypical one because the ADHD brain is always hunting for dopamine.

[Download: Managing and Safeguarding Your Child’s Screen Time].

A 2023 meta-analysis of more than 81,000 children found that two or more hours a day of screen time were associated with significantly elevated ADHD risk compared with less than two hours.1 Large longitudinal data from a separate study, which tracked more than 10,000 kids for two years, found that more screen time predicted increased ADHD – and that changes in brain structure helped explain the link.2.

Imaging research has tied greater screen time to altered development in the orbitofrontal cortex, lateral prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex – the regions that govern attention, cognitive control, and reward.

Back in the 1950s, the psychologist B.F. Skinner discovered something the entire tech industry would later weaponize: The most powerful way to drive a behavior isn’t to reward it every time, but to reward it unpredictably. It’s called a variable-ratio reinforcement schedule, and it’s the most addictive reward pattern known to behavioral science.

Sources indicate that it is why slot machines are built as they are. You pull the lever, and you might get nothing, or you might hit the jackpot. Not knowing is what keeps you pulling.

[Read: How Can I Help My Teen Better Manage Screen Time?].

According to recent reports, the same mechanism is now built into the games and apps your child uses every day. The loot box that might contain something rare. The next Roblox round that might go better. The Snapchat notification that might be from someone who matters. The Fortnite match that might end in a Victory Royale. The brain releases dopamine in anticipation of the reward, not when it arrives. This is why your child can’t stop.

But disconnect the device, and the compulsion largely collapses: the variable rewards stop, the social pressure disappears, and the relentless loop finally ends. You don’t have to eliminate every screen, but you must control the connection.

It has been revealed that the brain’s prefrontal cortex (the executive function center) isn’t fully developed until around age 25, and perhaps later in an individual with ADHD. Every year you delay access to the Internet is another year of maturity for your child’s executive function system before it’s asked to regulate the most dysregulating product ever made.

In a recent development, this is why a growing chorus of researchers is now urging parents to delay smartphones until at least high school (around age 14) and social media until at least age 16. The logic is simple: Let the most vulnerable period of brain development happen before your child can access the loop.

Here’s the empowering part: You control the devices, the accounts, the passwords, the router, and the timing of introduction. The strategy below is about exerting that control through environmental design – not nagging, not negotiating, not hoping a dysregulated brain suddenly regulates itself.

According to recent reports, STEP 1: Make a pact. Counter the “I’m the only one without a phone” argument by encouraging three or four other families to agree to delay access together. Ask the parents of your child’s friends to make the pact. It’s easier to hold the line together than alone.

According to recent reports, STEP 2: Stop competing with the screen. Control access to the dopamine source through environmental design, not willpower. Screens go in a central location after a certain hour. Devices charge outside bedrooms, every night, no exceptions.

STEP 3: Build “earn-access” systems. Screens become available only after the non-negotiables are done. Homework must be completed, then Xbox. Follow the simple, consistent rules every single day. The structure does the work so you don’t have to glitch the reminder.

Michael McLeod is the founder of GrowNOW ADHD and the author of The Executive Function Playbook.

#160666. How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3384 w)
